name: Learn: CIS Benchmarks (kube-bench)
description: Learn to audit a cluster against the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark with kube-bench, read its [PASS]/[FAIL]/[WARN] output, and remediate the most common node-level findings on a real multi-node cluster: control-plane manifest permissions, the kubelet read-only port, the apiserver NodeRestriction admission plugin, and PKI key permissions.
objective: CKS › Cluster Setup + System Hardening (10% + 15%). Goal: run kube-bench to audit nodes against the CIS Benchmark, interpret its findings, then remediate the recurring exam items — manifest/PKI file modes, the kubelet read-only port, and the NodeRestriction admission plugin.

questions.title: Run kube-bench against a node
questions.teach:
**kube-bench** (by Aqua Security) checks a Kubernetes node against the **CIS Kubernetes Benchmark** — a published list of hardening controls. Each control reports `[PASS]`, `[FAIL]`, or `[WARN]` (a `[WARN]` is usually a manual check it can't verify automatically, so you must inspect it by hand). On the CKS exam you run it, read the numbered findings (e.g. `1.1.1`), and remediate the `[FAIL]`s. Below each result block kube-bench prints a **Remediations** section with the exact fix — read it.

**How to run it** (kube-bench inspects the host's files and processes, so it must run **on the node** with the host mounted in):
- **As a Job/Pod** with the `aquasec/kube-bench` image, `hostPID: true`, and hostPath mounts for `/etc`, `/var` (what this step does). Read findings from the pod's **logs**.
- **As a binary** straight on the node: `kube-bench run` — fastest if you already have a shell on the host.
- **Via `docker run`** with the host bind-mounted — handy on kind where each node is a container.

**Targeting the right checks:**
- `--targets` selects sections: `master` (control-plane), `node` (kubelet/proxy), `etcd`, `policies`, `controlplane`. On a control-plane node you often want `--targets master,node`.
- kube-bench auto-detects the cluster version; override with `--version 1.29` or `--benchmark cis-1.9` if detection is wrong.
- Filter output with `grep` for `[FAIL]` / `[WARN]`, or add `--check 1.1.1` to run a single control.

**Gotchas:**
- A `[WARN]` is **not** a pass — it means kube-bench couldn't verify it; the exam may still expect a manual fix.
- Run on the **node itself**; a plain pod without `hostPID`/hostPath mounts reads the container's filesystem, not the host, and gives bogus results.
- Findings are **node-type specific**: master checks (1.x, 3.x) only make sense on a control-plane node; node checks (4.x) on workers.
- The Job needs `restartPolicy: Never` (or `OnFailure`) — Jobs reject `Always`.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `cks-bench`, create a Job named `kube-bench` that runs the `aquasec/kube-bench:latest` image against the node (mount the host so it can inspect real files; `hostPID: true`). Wait for it to complete, then confirm its logs contain CIS findings.

Target: a Job `kube-bench` in `cks-bench` has a completed pod whose logs contain at least one of `[PASS]`, `[FAIL]`, or `[WARN]`.
questions.hint: Apply a Job with `restartPolicy: Never`, `hostPID: true`, and the aquasec/kube-bench image using args `["run","--targets","node"]`; mount hostPath volumes for `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml`, `/etc/kubernetes`, and `/etc/systemd`. Then `kubectl -n cks-bench logs job/kube-bench | grep -E '\[(PASS|FAIL|WARN)\]'`.
questions.solution:
kubectl create namespace cks-bench 2>/dev/null
kubectl apply -f - <<'YAML'
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: kube-bench
  namespace: cks-bench
spec:
  backoffLimit: 1
  template:
    spec:
      hostPID: true
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: kube-bench
        image: aquasec/kube-bench:latest
        command: ["kube-bench"]
        args: ["run", "--targets", "node"]
        volumeMounts:
        - { name: var-lib-kubelet, mountPath: /var/lib/kubelet, readOnly: true }
        - { name: etc-kubernetes, mountPath: /etc/kubernetes, readOnly: true }
        - { name: etc-systemd, mountPath: /etc/systemd, readOnly: true }
      volumes:
      - { name: var-lib-kubelet, hostPath: { path: /var/lib/kubelet } }
      - { name: etc-kubernetes, hostPath: { path: /etc/kubernetes } }
      - { name: etc-systemd, hostPath: { path: /etc/systemd } }
YAML
kubectl -n cks-bench wait --for=condition=complete job/kube-bench --timeout=120s
kubectl -n cks-bench logs job/kube-bench | grep -E '\[(PASS|FAIL|WARN)\]' | head

verification.description: Job kube-bench completed and its logs contain CIS [PASS]/[FAIL]/[WARN] findings

questions.title: Remediate a file-permission FAIL
questions.teach:
A classic kube-bench `[FAIL]` is a static pod manifest under `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/` that is group/world readable. CIS requires these owned `root:root` with mode `0600`, because they contain sensitive flags (cert paths, tokens, admission config). Changing a manifest's **mode** does not restart its pod (the kubelet only re-reads the file's *contents*), so this is safe on a live cluster. On a kind cluster each node is a container — reach it with `docker exec <node>`.

**The two things CIS checks on these files — know both:**
- **Mode** — fix with `chmod`. `chmod 600 file` = `rw-------` (owner read/write only). `chmod 644` = `rw-r--r--` (the failing state). `stat -c '%a' file` prints the octal mode.
- **Ownership** — fix with `chown root:root file`. `stat -c '%U:%G' file` prints owner:group. A FAIL can be about owner, not just mode.

**Which files/dirs CIS flags (section 1.1), with their required modes:**
- Static pod manifests (`kube-apiserver.yaml`, `kube-controller-manager.yaml`, `kube-scheduler.yaml`, `etcd.yaml`) → `600`.
- The manifests directory itself and `/etc/kubernetes/pki` dir → `700` (dirs, not files).
- `admin.conf`, `scheduler.conf`, `controller-manager.conf` kubeconfigs → `600`.
- The etcd data dir (`/var/lib/etcd`) → `700`.

**Gotchas:**
- `chmod 600` on a manifest is non-disruptive; `chmod 600` on a *config the process actively reads at runtime* can still be fine, but never `chmod 000`.
- Symbolic modes work too (`chmod u=rw,go= file`), but octal is less error-prone — the grader checks the exact octal (`600`), so don't leave it at `640` or `0600`-with-a-leading-digit confusion (`stat -c '%a'` drops the leading zero and prints `600`).
- Dirs need the execute bit to be traversable: a dir is `700`/`755`, never `600`.
questions.prompt:
kube-bench flagged the kube-scheduler manifest on control-plane node `$CP`: it was left world/group readable at mode `644`. Set `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml` on `$CP` to exactly mode `600`.

Target: `docker exec $CP stat -c '%a' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml` prints `600`.
questions.solution:
docker exec $CP chmod 600 /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml
docker exec $CP stat -c '%a %U:%G' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml   # 600 root:root

questions.title: Harden the kubelet (read-only port)
questions.teach:
The kubelet can serve an **unauthenticated read-only port** (`10255`) that leaks pod and node metadata to anyone who can reach it. kube-bench flags this under the kubelet section (CIS 4.2.x). CIS requires it disabled by setting `readOnlyPort: 0` in the kubelet config. `0` disables the port entirely.

**Where the kubelet gets its settings — this is the exam trap:** a setting can come from the **config file** *or* a **command-line flag**, and the flag wins.
- **Config file** (preferred, used here): `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml` (a `KubeletConfiguration` object). Set `readOnlyPort: 0`.
- **CLI flag**: `--read-only-port=0` in the kubelet unit (`/etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/10-kubeadm.conf` / `/var/lib/kubelet/kubeadm-flags.env`). If a flag is set it **overrides** the config file — check both.

**Other kubelet hardening items CIS flags in the same file (good to recognize):**
- `authentication.anonymous.enabled: false` (no anonymous auth).
- `authorization.mode: Webhook` (not `AlwaysAllow`).
- `authentication.x509.clientCAFile` set (so kubelet can verify client certs).
- `protectKernelDefaults: true`, `makeIPTablesUtilChains: true`, `eventRecordQPS`, `streamingConnectionIdleTimeout`, `tlsCipherSuites`.

**Gotchas:**
- Kubelet config changes need a **`systemctl restart kubelet`** to take effect — editing the file alone does nothing.
- After the restart **wait for the node to go `Ready`** again (~15-20s). A broken edit (bad YAML, wrong field) can keep the kubelet down → node `NotReady`; check with `systemctl status kubelet` / `journalctl -u kubelet`.
- YAML is indentation-sensitive: `readOnlyPort` is a top-level key in the config, not nested.
- Don't confuse the read-only port (`10255`, unauthenticated) with the healthz port or the authenticated kubelet API port (`10250`).
questions.prompt:
On worker `$W1` the kubelet is serving its read-only port (seeded as `readOnlyPort: 10255`). Edit `/var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml` on `$W1` so that `readOnlyPort: 0`, then restart the kubelet. Give the node ~20s to report `Ready` again.

Target: the config on `$W1` has `readOnlyPort: 0` AND node `$W1` is `Ready`.
questions.hint: `docker exec $W1 sed -i 's/^readOnlyPort:.*/readOnlyPort: 0/' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml`, then `docker exec $W1 systemctl restart kubelet`.
questions.solution:
docker exec $W1 sed -i 's/^readOnlyPort:.*/readOnlyPort: 0/' /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml
docker exec $W1 grep readOnlyPort /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml   # readOnlyPort: 0
docker exec $W1 systemctl restart kubelet
kubectl get node $W1   # wait ~20s for Ready

verification.description: node $W1 is still Ready after the kubelet restart

questions.title: Harden the apiserver (NodeRestriction)
questions.teach:
`NodeRestriction` is a kube-apiserver admission plugin that limits what each kubelet can modify to **only its own Node object and the Pods bound to it** — so a compromised node cannot tamper with other nodes or escalate. kube-bench checks that it is enabled via the `--enable-admission-plugins` flag on the kube-apiserver static pod manifest.

**How admission plugins are configured on the apiserver:**
- `--enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction,...` — a **comma-separated** list; to add one, append `,NodeRestriction` to the existing value (don't drop the others). If the flag is absent, add it as a new arg line under the container `command`.
- `--disable-admission-plugins=...` turns off defaults. Several plugins (`NamespaceLifecycle`, `ServiceAccount`, etc.) are **on by default** even without the flag — `NodeRestriction` is *not* enabled by default for older setups, so CIS requires it explicitly.
- Some plugins need a config file via `--admission-control-config-file` (e.g. `PodSecurity`, `EventRateLimit`, `ImagePolicyWebhook`). Others CKS cares about: `AlwaysPullImages`, `PodSecurity`.

**Editing a static pod manifest — the mechanics:** the file lives in `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/`; the kubelet **watches** it and automatically recreates the apiserver pod when the file changes. There is no `kubectl apply` — you edit the file in place.

**Gotchas:**
- A typo or bad indentation takes the **apiserver down**, so `kubectl` stops working entirely. Keep a backup (`cp kube-apiserver.yaml /tmp/`) before editing.
- After saving, the apiserver takes ~15-30s to restart; `kubectl` will error with connection-refused meanwhile — wait, don't panic-edit.
- Flags are **one per YAML list item** under `command:` — merge values into the existing `--enable-admission-plugins` line rather than adding a duplicate flag (a duplicate flag makes the apiserver refuse to start).
- Verify against the **running** apiserver, not just the file: `kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-$CP -o yaml | grep admission` (or `crictl`/`ps` on the node if the API is down).
questions.prompt:
Setup removed `NodeRestriction` from the apiserver's `--enable-admission-plugins`. Edit `/etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml` on `$CP` so the flag includes `NodeRestriction` again (keep any other plugins), then wait for the apiserver to come back.

Target: the running kube-apiserver has `NodeRestriction` in `--enable-admission-plugins`.
questions.hint: `docker exec -it $CP bash`, then add the line `- --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction` under the kube-apiserver command args (or append `,NodeRestriction` to an existing value). Save and wait ~20s for the apiserver to restart.
questions.solution:
# Setup removed the flag line, so add it back under the kube-apiserver args:
docker exec $CP sed -i '/^    - kube-apiserver$/a\    - --enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
# (If the flag already exists with other plugins, instead append ,NodeRestriction to its value.)
# Wait ~20s for the apiserver to restart, then verify:
kubectl -n kube-system get pod kube-apiserver-$CP -o yaml | grep enable-admission-plugins

questions.title: Protect PKI private-key permissions
questions.teach:
The cluster's PKI lives under `/etc/kubernetes/pki/` on the control-plane. The **private keys** (`ca.key`, `apiserver.key`, etc.) are the crown jewels — anyone who reads `ca.key` can mint certificates for *any* identity in the cluster. kube-bench requires private keys to be mode `0600` (owner read/write only) and owned `root:root`. Fixing the mode is non-disruptive: it changes the file's permission bits, not its contents, so nothing restarts.

**CIS splits PKI permissions into two rules (CIS 1.1.21 = private keys, 1.1.20 = certificate files) — don't mix them up:**
- **Private keys** (`*.key`) → mode `0600` (`rw-------`): only root may read them.
- **Certificates** (`*.crt`) → mode `0644` is acceptable (`rw-r--r--`): certs are public, so world-readable is fine; they just must not be world-*writable*.
- The `pki` **directory** itself → `0700`.
- All PKI files owned `root:root` (check with `stat -c '%U:%G'`).

**A one-liner that fixes every key at once:** `find /etc/kubernetes/pki -name '*.key' -exec chmod 600 {} \;` (and `-name '*.crt' -exec chmod 644 {} \;` for certs).

**Gotchas:**
- `chmod 600` on a `.key` is safe and never restarts anything; but don't accidentally `chmod 600` a `.crt` that another component reads as a non-root user, or `chmod 000` anything.
- `stat -c '%a'` prints `600` (no leading zero) — that's the graded value; `640` or `660` still leak the key to the group and will FAIL.
- Don't forget **ownership**: a key can be `600` but owned by a non-root user and still FAIL the CIS owner check — set both mode and `root:root`.
questions.prompt:
kube-bench flagged `/etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.key` on `$CP`: setup loosened it to mode `644`. Set it back to exactly mode `600`.

Target: `docker exec $CP stat -c '%a' /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.key` prints `600`.
questions.solution:
docker exec $CP chmod 600 /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.key
docker exec $CP stat -c '%a %U:%G' /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.key   # 600 root:root
